newsitem.title: FRANCE: French election policies missing in action.
newsitem.headline: French election policies missing in action.

text.p: When French Socialist leader Lionel Jospin suggested looking in a "lost-and-found" office for the centre-right government's policies, Prime Minister Alain Juppe retorted that his rival had nothing more than a few slogans to offer.
The jibes sum up the tone ahead of the two-round election on May 25 and June 1 that has left French voters disillusioned and doubtful about whether there are any real choices on offer.
Even Jospin and Juppe -- widely regarded as uninspiring leaders -- acknowledge their policies are hard to sell.

"I have no magic wand," Juppe told a campaign lunch in the rural hamlet of Sainte-Croix de Mareuil, where the party faithful had broken off from their foie gras to greet the prime minister with cries of "Juppe, Juppe" as he arrived.
"French people doubt the ability of politics to change the course of events," Jospin wrote in daily Liberation.

"Their scepticism towards the programmes of the different political movements, especially on economic and social policy, is one of the most serious signs of the confidence crisis in this country," he said.
In reality, economists say, neither side has much room for manoeuvre if France is to shape up its public finances for European monetary union in January 1999.
President Jacques Chirac advanced the election by nearly a year promising a "nouvel elan" in French politics, but few expect more than a new shine on old shoes.
The mainstream parties are both committed to launching a single currency in January 1999 -- meaning further austerity from the right, and at least some belt-tightening from the left.
Neither side has offered any miracle cure to France's biggest woe, unemployment at a postwar record of 12.8 percent.
Both want, in their own way, to free up the workforce -- the left through cutting the legal working week, the right through more labour market flexibility.

But while employer resistance and a need to keep France competitive in the free trade world under "globalisation" will hamstring the left, the threat of social unrest is likely to keep at bay any radical departure by the right.
Juppe already had to backtrack on some of his reforms in 1995 after a paralysing public sector strike.

While the left pledges to halt sales of state-owned companies, and the right to privatise, they share a common vision of France where a benevolent state and universal welfare system remain the guarantee of individual rights.
Given the apathy, politicians are already wary of massive abstentions, especially in the first round vote.

"Some are still hesitating, some are not very happy -- I understand their discontent -- and they could be tempted to show their bad mood in the first round, and go on a Sunday outing when it comes to the second round," Juppe said in an appeal last Thursday in this southwestern Dordogne hamlet.
The worry for the mainstream parties is that apathy or a protest vote can only help the extreme-right National Front, with its simple, populist message that immigration has cost French people jobs.

Opinion polls have shown the National Front winning up to 15 percent of votes, compared to 37-40 percent for the centre-right RPR/UDF coalition, around 25-26 percent for the Socialist party and about 10 percent for the Communist Party.
On top of indifference to their policies, Jospin and Juppe may lack the charisma to lure the voters out in big numbers.
Juppe, though admired by Chirac and many in his own party as an able technocrat, acknowledges himself that he is "a bit dry" for many voters, and opinion polls show he is deeply unpopular.
"Everyone says I'm an insensitive computer, so I don't know why you are asking," he told a radio interviewer.
Criticism of Juppe has almost become so much of a joke in the campaign that he might even get the sympathy vote.
"If we wanted a sexy leader we would not have chosen Juppe" one of his followers said at a rally in Bordeaux, provoking a chant of "Juppe, Juppe" from the 2,000-strong crowd.
Jospin, though respected for his honesty, is not a populist leader, and prefers to stress integrity rather than bank on the kind of media blaze that helped Britain's Labour Party to power.
